meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Even if you're on the right track, you'll get run over if you just sit there'?
meta.ogDescription: Earliest documented use is the syndicated column 'Tom Sims Says', 7 March 1925. Will Rogers was credited only in 1970, 35 years after his death.

answer.label: Not Will Rogers — most likely Tom Sims
answer.authorDates: American newspaper humorist · syndicated NEA columnist of the 1920s
answer.sourceLine: Will Rogers did not write this. Quote Investigator traces the earliest known instance to a syndicated column of one-line jokes, “Tom Sims Says,” printed on 7 March 1925 in papers including The Sheboygan Press of Wisconsin and The Indianapolis Times of Indiana, and concludes that “Tom Sims is the most likely creator of this quip.” The Will Rogers credit is first documented in Forbes on 15 November 1970 — thirty-five years after Rogers died.

source.heading: The earliest documented source

docMeta.dd: The Sheboygan Press (Wisconsin), p. 24, and The Indianapolis Times (Indiana), p. 4 — syndicated by the Newspaper Enterprise Association
Will Rogers — first documented in Forbes, 15 November 1970

source.excerpt:
The straight and narrow path is plenty wide for its traffic.
Even if you are on the right track you will get run over if you just sit there.
Love is blind. But there is always some friend who thinks he is an eye doctor.
trail: Anchor: Quote Investigator finds the earliest match in the syndicated column “Tom Sims Says” of 7 March 1925, printed in The Sheboygan Press of Wisconsin and The Indianapolis Times of Indiana, and states that “Tom Sims is the most likely creator of this quip.”

The joke spread and shed its author within a week: QI documents the same-day reprint headed “Smile-A-While” in The Saginaw News Courier, a 9 March 1925 printing in The Columbia Record credited only to the Newspaper Enterprise Association, and a 13 March 1925 reprint in The News-Herald of Franklin, Pennsylvania with an acknowledgement but no name.

The Will Rogers credit arrives long afterwards. Rogers died in 1935, per Wikipedia; the first Rogers ascription QI locates is a Forbes page of 15 November 1970, and QI concludes that “the time delay in both cases was excessive; hence, these two attributions were not substantive.”
Reading Wikiquote’s Will Rogers page confirms the line appears in neither its sourced quotations nor its Misattributed section — it has never had a foothold in the documented Rogers corpus at all.
source.excerptNote: Three consecutive items from the syndicated column “Tom Sims Says” of 7 March 1925, as transcribed by Quote Investigator — the earliest instance located anywhere. The line was one gag among several, not a maxim.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full 1925 citation trail

source.rightsNote: The wording originates in a United States newspaper column syndicated on 7 March 1925 — comfortably before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — so the sentence itself is in the public domain. The later reprints, variants and celebrity attributions from 1970 onward create no new rights in a line already published in 1925.

author.name: Tom Sims
author.heading: Tom Sims
author.metaLine: American newspaper humorist · syndicated NEA columnist of the 1920s
author.bio: Tom Sims wrote “Tom Sims Says,” a column of miscellaneous jokes and observations distributed to American newspapers in the 1920s by the Newspaper Enterprise Association — the kind of daily filler that quietly supplied the language with a great many of its proverbs. Quote Investigator gives no biography of him, but the NEA humorist of that name is almost certainly the Tom Sims whom comics reference works date 1896–1972 and credit as the writer who took over the Thimble Theatre (Popeye) strip after E. C. Segar’s death in 1938. Either way, the line belongs to a working columnist filing copy by the inch, not to the famous humorist it drifted onto forty-five years later.

misattribution.heading: How Will Rogers got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is the classic pattern for a magnet name: an ownerless newspaper quip, funny and folksy, drifts onto the most famous folksy American available. The line was in print for forty-five years before anyone thought to put Rogers’s name on it.

items.why: Rogers died in 1935. The earliest Rogers ascription QI can find is a Forbes “Thoughts On the Business of Life” page of 15 November 1970, followed by a 29 November 1970 clothing-store advertisement in Allentown’s Sunday Call-Chronicle, then quotation books in 1977 and 1992. It is absent from the sourced and misattributed lists on Wikiquote’s Rogers page alike.

Twain died in 1910. QI dates the first Twain credit to a 12 August 1984 Philadelphia Inquirer advertisement for Gwynedd-Mercy College, repeated in The Gazette of Montreal in May 1985 — seventy-four years after his death, and fifty-nine after the line was already in newsprint.

Orlando’s Sentinel Star ran the line over the broadcaster’s name on 9 September 1975, per QI — a useful tell, since a saying that collects three unrelated celebrities in fifteen years almost never belongs to any of them.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented instance is Tom Sims’s syndicated column “Tom Sims Says” of 7 March 1925, and Quote Investigator concludes that Sims “is the most likely creator of this quip” — not Will Rogers, not Mark Twain, not Arthur Godfrey.

context.heading: How an unsigned newspaper joke found a famous voice
lead: The 1925 newspaper page ran on filler, and Tom Sims filed it by the column-inch: three or four unrelated one-liners a day, syndicated nationwide by the Newspaper Enterprise Association. Quote Investigator shows how quickly a good one slipped its author — the same day it ran under Sims’s name in Sheboygan and Indianapolis, it appeared in Saginaw under the different heading “Smile-A-While”; two days later The Columbia Record printed it credited only to the syndicate; and one week later a Pennsylvania paper reprinted it with an acknowledgement and no author at all.

Once a saying is orphaned it needs a voice, and mid-century America had a stock one: the drawling cowboy philosopher. Nothing links the line to Will Rogers except that it sounds like him. Per QI’s trail, the first credit to Rogers is a Forbes “Thoughts On the Business of Life” page dated 15 November 1970, and from there it moved into a clothing-store advertisement two weeks later, then into the quotation dictionaries that make an attribution permanent.
detailsBody: Sims himself did not treat the line as scripture. QI records that in his 29 June 1925 column he simply rewrote it: “Being on the right track is correct. But if you just stop there you’ll get run over.” Other papers kept reshaping it too — “it’s probable you’ll get run over” in The Atlanta Constitution in December 1925, “you’re liable to get run over” in The Film Daily in January 1931 — which is exactly how folk sayings behave and exactly how single-author quotations do not.

Rogers was not the only famous name to collect the line. QI documents a 1975 credit to broadcaster Arthur Godfrey in Orlando’s Sentinel Star, and a 1984 Mark Twain credit in a Philadelphia college advertisement. Twain died in 1910, which puts that one seventy-four years past the possible.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest match is the syndicated column "Tom Sims Says" of 7 March 1925 in The Sheboygan Press (WI, quote page 24) and The Indianapolis Times (IN, quote page 4); QI states "Tom Sims is the most likely creator of this quip" and "QI has found no substantive evidence supporting the attributions to Mark Twain and Will Rogers." QI also documents the same-day "Smile-A-While by Tom Sims" reprint in The Saginaw News Courier, the 9 March 1925 Columbia Record printing credited to the Newspaper Enterprise Association, the 13 March 1925 News-Herald (Franklin, PA) reprint with acknowledgement but no attribution, Sims's 29 June 1925 rewrite "Being on the right track is correct. But if you just stop there you'll get run over," the December 1925 Atlanta Constitution "probable" variant, the 26 January 1931 Film Daily "liable" variant, the first Will Rogers credit in Forbes of 15 November 1970 ("Thoughts On the Business of Life", quote page 96), the 29 November 1970 Sunday Call-Chronicle (Allentown) clothing-store advertisement crediting Rogers, the 9 September 1975 Arthur Godfrey credit in Orlando's Sentinel Star, the 1977 Peter's Quotations and 1992 And I Quote Rogers credits, the 12 August 1984 Philadelphia Inquirer Gwynedd-Mercy College advertisement crediting Mark Twain, and the 7 May 1985 Montreal Gazette Twain credit; and concludes "Will Rogers died in 1935, and he received credit by 1970. Mark Twain died in 1910, and he received credit by 1984. The time delay in both cases was excessive; hence, these two attributions were not substantive."

Wikiquote's Will Rogers page contains no instance of "right track", "run over" or "sit there" anywhere in its wikitext; its Misattributed section lists only the return-of-capital line, the "nice doggie" diplomacy line, "Don't let yesterday use up too much of today", and "You never get a second chance to make a good first impression".

Will Rogers was born 4 November 1879 and died 15 August 1935; he was an American humorist, newspaper columnist, vaudeville performer and film actor, and his syndicated newspaper column ran from 1922 to 1935.
Tom Sims was an American comics writer, 26 May 1896 to 15 December 1972, who took over the Thimble Theatre / Popeye newspaper comic strip following creator Elzie Segar's death in 1938.

The William G. Pomeroy Foundation historic marker reads: "TOM SIMS 1896-1972. ONE OF THE WRITERS OF 'POPEYE' COMIC, INSPIRED BY LIFE & PEOPLE ON COOSA RIVER INCLUDING FATHER, CAPTAIN OF GADSDEN STEAMBOAT 'LEOTA.'"

Goodreads hosts "Even if you are on the right track, you'll get run over if you just sit there." attributed to Will Rogers with no published source given, and states that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.
